name: Yara Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Northfield Surgery, on the edge of the city near the old railway works, which is where I grew up. It's a busy practice, lots of families, a lot of men with bad backs and bad chests from the works, and grandmothers bringing in grandchildren. I see about eighteen people in the morning and do baby checks and phone calls in the afternoon. I'm still finding my feet, and I ask Dr Fraser, the senior partner, about nearly every tricky case.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy knowing the families. I treated a lad last month whose grandad I'd met at church the week before. What wears me out is the computer, all the clicking and templates, and the forms. I'm engaged to Erik, an electrician, and we're getting married in the spring at our church, so that's most of my weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and good. Medicine is about people, and you can't put a computer in a front room with a grieving widow. I'd say it after church to anyone who asked, and I'd leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means life goes on as I'd planned. My job is safe, the pay is good, I've saved well, and Erik has steady work. We'd get married, move into his house on Clarence Street and hopefully start a family in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. I'd finish my training, keep learning the computer system bit by bit, and keep saving with Erik for the extension on his house for when the babies come. I wouldn't touch the AI tools, because there'd be no reason to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. Peaceful, really. It's the future I already pictured.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never touch the AI tools. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust what I can't check. If a computer writes my notes and gets it wrong, it's my name on it and my patient who suffers. I'd rather type slowly and know every word in a patient's notes is mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about Northfield that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dr Fraser is sixty-three, and when he retires the practice could be bought by one of the big health companies. They'd run it for profit with locum doctors who don't know anyone. That worries me more than any AI.

say: Medicine is about **people**, so I'm not surprised and I'm glad.
You can't put a **computer** in a front room with a grieving widow.
think: Life goes on **as planned**: safe job, good savings and Erik's steady work.
We'd marry, move into **his house** and start a family in a couple of years.
do: Finish my **training** and learn the computer system bit by bit.
Keep saving with Erik for an **extension** on his house.
Stay away from the **AI tools**, since there's no reason to use them.
feel: **Content** and peaceful, because it's the future she already pictured.
S0.quote: I'd rather type slowly and know every word in a patient's notes is mine.
fieldNote: She **doesn't trust** what she can't check, and wants every word in her notes to be hers.
Her bigger fear is a **corporate buyout** of the practice, not AI.
Her plans centre on **marriage, home and children**.

steps.text: Finish training and keep typing her own notes at Northfield
Save with Erik for an extension on his house on Clarence Street

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say be careful. I'd say at the practice that I'm happy for the computer to book appointments, but not to decide who's ill. I'd probably say it at church too, where a lot of the older ones are frightened of all this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd fall behind. If everyone else is using the AI to write letters and I'm not, the partners would notice I'm slower. But I think there'll always be room for a doctor who knows the families, and Northfield isn't a place that changes fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on doing it my way for the first year and see whether the tools actually stick. If the practice made it compulsory, I'd do the training, but only for letters and booking. I'd still examine every patient myself and write my own notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit stubborn, I'll admit. I don't like being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be most affected at Northfield, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat and Denise on reception, who've been there twenty years between them. Booking is the first thing the AI takes. They're not the type to retrain in computers, and they've got families depending on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd fall behind, but also that you'd do it your way. Is that a risk you'd take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because I can. I've got savings and there are three other practices within a short drive that would hire me. A slower doctor who knows your grandmother is worth more than a fast one who doesn't.

say: Be **careful**: let the computer book appointments, not decide who's ill.
I'd say the same at **church**, where older people are frightened of this.
think: I'd probably **fall behind** while others let AI write their letters.
There will always be room for a doctor who **knows the families**.
do: Carry on **my own way** for the first year and see if the tools stick.
Do compulsory training **only for letters** and booking if forced.
Keep **examining every patient** myself and writing my own notes.
feel: **Uneasy** and a bit stubborn, disliking being pushed.
S1.quote: A slower doctor who knows your grandmother is worth more than a fast one who doesn't.
fieldNote: She accepts being **slower** as a price worth paying, backed by savings and local jobs.
Her concern goes to the **receptionists**, whom she sees as first to lose work.
She draws a line between AI for **admin** and AI for medical judgement.

steps.text: Keep examining every patient herself and writing her own notes
Wait a year to see which AI tools Northfield actually keeps

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless, rushing something like this into people's health. I'd say the big tech firms and the government have no business deciding that a machine can be your doctor. I'd say it at work and at church, plainly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be frightened for my career. If the AI can diagnose better than me by 2028, the practice won't need a junior who still asks the senior partner about every tricky case. I'd still have examinations and baby checks until the robots come around 2031, but I'd be twenty-nine and only half-trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Erik and I would start a family straight away instead of waiting. His work as an electrician is hands-on, so it's safe until about 2031, and I could drop to part-time and do the baby clinics and home visits. We'd cut back, no new car, no big holidays, and I'd lean on my mum and his parents for help with childcare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Sad, too, because I worked so hard for this. But I'd have faith we'd get through it as a family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum the night it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum that her daughter the doctor might end up being mostly a mother, and that's not the worst thing in the world. She'd cry, because she was so proud at my graduation. Then she'd put the kettle on and start planning a nursery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Erik's work is safe until about 2031. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, honestly. Maybe robots wire houses by then, maybe they don't, and someone has to fix the robots. I'd rather trust my husband's hands and our family than a government cheque.

say: Rushing this into health care is **reckless**.
Big tech and government have **no business** deciding a machine can be your doctor.
think: The practice won't need a **junior** who still asks about every tricky case.
I'd keep **examinations and baby checks** until 2031, but only half-trained.
do: Start a **family** with Erik straight away instead of waiting.
Drop to **part-time** baby clinics and home visits.
Cut back on a **new car** and holidays, and lean on our parents.
feel: **Anxious** and sad after working so hard, but with faith in her family.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum that her daughter the doctor might end up being mostly a mother, and that's not the worst thing in the world.
fieldNote: She'd **bring children forward**, relying on her fiancé's hands-on trade.
She blames **big tech and government** together, not one side.
She prefers **family support** over any government payment.

steps.text: Start a family with Erik straight away instead of waiting
Skip the new car and big holidays this year
Ask her mum and Erik's parents to help with childcare

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is still too fast, but at least people can prepare. I'd tell the young ones at church to learn a trade or something with their hands. At work I'd ask the partners what their plan is, straight out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes it less frightening. I'd be fully trained by 2029 and thirty-two when it arrives, and the hands-on work like baby checks, smear tests and maternity care lasts until about 2034. I'd probably have a little one by then, too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd steer my training toward women's health and care of mothers and babies: antenatal checks, baby clinics, contraception fittings. Those are hands-on and close to families, which suits me. We'd still marry in the spring and plan our first baby for 2028, and we'd save hard in the meantime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened. I feel there's a road through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years change your mind about using the AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, near the end, for letters. But I'd still not let it make a decision about a patient. My grandmother used to say a good doctor uses her eyes and her hands, and I believe that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Northfield would you worry about in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pat and Denise again, and Dr Fraser, if he hasn't retired. He's brilliant but he can barely send an email. I'd want the practice to let him finish with dignity, not push him out with a computer.

say: Five years is **still too fast**, but people can at least prepare.
Young people should **learn a trade** or something with their hands.
think: I'd be **fully trained** and thirty-two when it arrives.
Hands-on work like **baby checks** and maternity care lasts until about 2034.
do: Steer my training toward **women's health** and care of mothers and babies.
Marry in the spring and plan our **first baby** for 2028.
feel: **Uneasy, not frightened**, with a road through it.
S3.quote: My grandmother used to say a good doctor uses her eyes and her hands, and I believe that.
fieldNote: She chooses **maternity and baby care**, matching hands-on skills to her values.
Her trust rests on **eyes and hands**, a phrase from her grandmother.
She wants older colleagues to **finish with dignity**.

steps.text: Focus her training on antenatal checks, baby clinics and contraception fittings
Plan their first baby for 2028 after the spring wedding
Save hard with Erik until the baby arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do it properly, slowly and safely. I'd tell people not to panic and to keep their families close. That's what I'd say to anyone who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's fine. I'd be thirty-seven in 2036, a trained family doctor with children, and the hands-on work would last until about 2039. By then, I hope, I'm doing mostly baby clinics and home visits, the bits no one wants a machine for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the plan: marry, train, start a family. I'd keep saving with Erik so we've got a good cushion by the time the children are at school. I wouldn't change my habits around AI until I saw it working properly in other practices for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's far enough away that I can just live my life. I'd say a prayer about it now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your own children about work, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands, like their dad, because an electrician's trade has fed families for generations. A robot that can rewire an old house is a long way off. I'd want them to know how to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't change your habits. Is there any risk in that, with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes. If I'm still refusing the tools in 2035, I might be the doctor nobody wants to hire. But I'd rather be late and careful than early and wrong, and ten years gives me time to change my mind.

say: Ten years is time to do it **properly**, slowly and safely.
Don't **panic**, and keep your families close.
think: By 2036 I'd be a **trained doctor** with children.
I hope to be doing mostly **baby clinics** and home visits by then.
do: Carry on with the plan to **marry, train** and start a family.
Keep saving with Erik for a **good cushion** by school age.
Wait to use AI until it has **worked for years** elsewhere.
feel: **Calm**, because it's far enough away to just live her life.
S4.quote: I'd tell my children to learn something with their hands, like their dad, because an electrician's trade has fed families for generations.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her put **family first** without changing her plans.
She admits **refusing tools** until 2035 could make her hard to hire.
She'd steer her children toward **trades**, like her electrician fiancé.

steps.text: Marry, finish training and start a family as planned
Save with Erik for a cushion by the time children start school
Hold off on AI tools until other practices have used them for years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be half-trained, just married, and everything I worked for would be thrown up in the air at once. What would help is the practices keeping doctors for the hands-on work and the families, and letting young doctors like me go part-time without losing our place.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith or family much. That's what gets people round here through hard times, not apps or schemes. When the railway works shut, it was the church and the families that held people together, not the government.

headlineQuote: When the railway works shut, it was the church and the families that held people together, not the government.
portrait: Yara is a **27-year-old junior doctor** at Northfield, a busy practice near the old railway works where she grew up.
She's **engaged to Erik**, an electrician, and plans a church wedding and children soon.
She **never uses AI tools** and trusts her own eyes, hands and typed notes.
Her mood rises to **anxious** with two-year AGI, when she'd bring children forward and go part-time.
She trusts **family, faith and trades** over government help or big tech.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when she'd be half-trained and newly married with her career thrown into the air.
whatWouldHelp: Practices keeping doctors for **hands-on care** and families.
Letting young doctors go **part-time** without losing their place.
